The story of Borderlands 1 is a great tragedy about ennui, nihilism, the Lovecraftian insanity of living forever against your will. The cover art is of a psycho committing suicide, but without a gun he can only pretend with his fingers. Instead of blood, the world of Pandora splatters out the back of his head.

You get off a bus with pretty much no backstory. Where did you come from? No idea. Before you even touch dirt, a handler contacts you and starts guiding you through the story. Someone's watching - someone's always watching.

You learn about the New U machine, which recreates you when you die, for a small fee. But here's the kicker: if you don't have the money, they still do it for free. There really isn't any way to die. You can't refuse a New U recreation, they just do it.

The bandits will also respawn when you kill them, but they appear to be on a shittier version of the New U service - it takes them about an hour to be recreated. So why are there gravestones in Fyrestone? Evidently some people are allowed to die, while others aren't. This doesn't have anything to do with money, at least not for you. For the bandits, it certainly doesn't have anything to do with following the law. But for the law-abiding citizens of Fyrestone, something they did disqualified them from a New U service. And they died permanently. Maybe they just found a way out.

Then you enter Fyrestone and liberate the single citizen. (Sound similar to Liar's Berg? Hmm. Commonalities...) You shoot some bandits and skags, then go meet TK Baha. TK has you go loot his wife's grave for guns and kill bandits. Then, when you turn in the quest, you hear him say "My wife would be so proud right now! If only I could remember her name..." How long would you have to die and respawn before you forgot your own wife's name? This has been going on for many, many years, it seems. And memory loss is part of it.

All of a sudden, the cryptic statements by many of the NPCs start to make more sense... Don't worry about saying goodbye; I'm sure we'll all be doing this again soon enough.

I believe the recreation process has a small (0.01% maybe?) chance of botching the job, and recreating your body improperly. This is a wonderful explanation of why there are so many midgets, brutes, Badass psychos and Goliaths out there. No normal reproductive process could survive that high a mutation rate - it must be a side effect of being recreated hundreds of times a year.

Later on in the game when you talk to Tannis, she says the Vault only opens once every 200 years - spoiler! When you rescue Tannis from her jail cell, if you stop to read the writing on the wall, you can see she's working on some sort of theory that reality is cyclical and repeats regularly. Use a scoped weapon and you can read most of it.

We also uncover history of Pandora through Tannis' logs. She mentions that Dahl was making good money by mining eridium on Pandora, and they were using prisoners as cheap labor. Then, for no reason, they just up and left. They didn't bother to take the prisoners with them. Everybody but the CEOs got left on Pandora to fend for themselves. Except, of course, they still couldn't die.

It is also mentioned that Atlas got to the top of the corporation heap by using alien technology in their guns - we don't see any of that, Atlas guns are just particularly well-manufactured guns, for the most part. But this tells us that Pandora (and possibly other planets with alien technology) are being fought over by the corporations!

Finally, near the end, we open the Vault and the crescendo of mystery never really gets unraveled. What was Dahl and Hyperion doing reconstructing everybody for so long? Why didn't Dahl take their cheap labor and move them to another planet to continue making money off them? There is obviously some kind of purpose behind causing so much perpetual lawlessness and carnage here on Pandora.

It's very possible that Hyperion and Dahl found what they were looking for on Pandora. Leaving their criminal workers on Pandora and constantly recreating them is a way of creating an embedded hostile force on Pandora which would resist Atlas or any other rival corporation from finding and exploiting the resources that Dahl and Hyperion had uncovered, and it's even possible that Dahl and Hyperion programmed the Vault to go to the Destroyer upon opening, to kill anyone who might be on to the same trail as they were. It doesn't make a whole lot of sense and there are a lot of unanswered questions.

This theory is supported in many ways by BL2, in which Atlas as a company is dismantled and no longer seen from. Many other corporations disappear from the public listings. (S&S, you will be missed.) In BL2 we see Hyperion showcasing a new game-changing recoil system, which could be derived from alien technology they uncovered. Dahl really hasn't improved their design much, so it's possible they got the short end of the stick.

When, at the end of BL2, we see hints of the Vault being some kind of transporation system it begins to becomes more clear. Dahl and Hyperion sabotaged the first Vault to deter anyone else from uncovering what they've found - which may be a transplanetary teleportation system left over from the aliens!

BL2 also raises more questions - for example, more people die in BL2 and there are other strong themes of corporations oppressing people and the cheapness of human life. BL1 had strong themes of loneliness and isolation, which BL2 really didn't share.

So, this is turning out to be a lot harder to answer than I would have thought. I'm trying to think about what I don't like about the game and then look at those things from the perspective of someone completely new to it and that's really throwing me!

I think what it boils down to at this point is community or lack there of. WoW used to be the benchmark for the MM in MMOs; race/faction capital cities were PACKED with players hanging around, showing off gear, chatting, trading and just generally interacting. The chat channels were constant and lively (quality of content was another matter) and the gameworld just generally felt alive and populated. In this most recent expansion, Blizzard introduced garrisons which became de facto single person capital cities. Within your garrison you could construct buildings that housed your profession trainers, bankers, auctioneers and basically everything else that you would go to a capital city for. Garrisons allowed you to send out followers on missions that rewarded you with loot equivalent in stats to what you'd find in dungeons, removing any real impetus to group up and run them. Mines and gardens in the garrisons removed the need to go out hunting for ore and herbs and people just generally now log in, send followers on missions/collect mission rewards, and afk while waiting to raid.

Now, the garrison only shows up once you've hit level 92. So what, you may ask, does this have to do with someone levelling their first character? Well, it means that you're in for a long, lonely slog to 100. There's very little to interest most veteran players aside from endgame raiding, so you rarely see many people out questing. The impressively massive cities like Orgrimmar, Stormwind and Ironforge are disappointingly empty and the game just feels lacking because of it.

I unsubscribed about a month ago. I'm hoping that Blizzard shakes it off and comes back with something extraordinary that re-enlivens the game and the community for the next expansion, but until then I'd suggest looking into something else like SW:TOR or Wildstar.
